title: A hybrid logical clock rewritten with max(), proved to never go backwards on any input
summary: The receive rule of a hybrid logical clock has four branches; a developer rewrites it as one `max` and two conditionals. The property the clock exists for, that the new timestamp is later than both the last one and the message's and never behind the physical clock, is proved for every pair of 64-bit timestamps and every wall-clock reading. The refactor is merged on the strength of the proof, not of a review of the branches.

change.description: Compute the physical part as the maximum of the three physical parts, then derive the counter: continue the last timestamp's counter if the last timestamp had that physical part, and take the larger of that and the message's counter if the message had it too. The four-way branch becomes three lines.

risk: None, and that is the point: a verifier that only fails builds is switched off. The receive rule is the one place where two clocks and a wall clock meet, the kind of code a reviewer re-derives by hand with a table of cases. Here the table is the prover's job. The properties in the file are the ones the paper proves for the algorithm (the clock is monotonic and stays within the physical clock's drift), and the proof covers the 2^47 physical values, the 2^16 counters and every combination of them, which no test and no review does.
explanation: The properties file states, for `receive`: on every input with a valid wall-clock reading and two well-formed timestamps whose counters are not exhausted, the result is greater than the last timestamp and the message's, its physical part is at least the wall clock, and it equals `receive(nowMillis, message, last)`, since the rule must not care which of the two timestamps is called "last". The last clause is a law stated by calling the method inside its own property. JBMC proves all of it over the three `long` parameters in about a second. For an equivalence-preserving refactor this is exactly the assurance wanted: the new code has the properties the old code was proved to have. (Example 018 is the same refactor with one case dropped, which the same property refutes.)
resolution: Merge. The properties did not change, so the pull request contains code only, and the proof is re-run on every build.
provenance: Constructed as the equivalent rewrite of the receive rule of Kulkarni et al., to pair with example 018.

references.title: Kulkarni, Demirbas, Madappa, Avva and Leone, Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases
